Coverage-Preserving Self-Healing in Partially Observable 3D UAV Swarm Networks via an Advection-Diffusion Graph TransformerThanks: Thanks:

Abstract

This paper investigates the resilience and self-healing of unmanned aerial vehicle swarm communication networks under severe network partitioning in complex and adversarial environments. To address limited global observability after damage, we develop a damage-state inference mechanism that enables the ground control station (GCS) to infer global failures from sparse local reports without transmitting location-sensitive coordinates. To recover multi-cluster partitioned topologies, we then propose AdDiff-GT, a physics-inspired graph Transformer that incorporates advection-diffusion dynamics into a node-supernode hybrid graph. Local message propagation captures intra-cluster structural relationships, while global attention models inter-cluster interactions. A weighted composite loss jointly considers connectivity restoration, maneuvering cost, motion consistency, inter-cluster coordination, and spatial preservation during model training. We further develop a meta-learning strategy for transferable initialization across damage patterns and swarm scales, enabling efficient online GCS adaptation and distributed airborne inference. Simulations on 8,000 partitioned scenarios, including 5,000 large-scale cases, show that AdDiff-GT achieves effective topology recovery and spatial preservation over six representative baselines. Meta-learning reduces online planning overhead with a minor increase in recovery steps, balancing prior knowledge transfer and online adaptation.

Index Terms: 
UAV swarm networks, resilient self-healing, advection-diffusion graph Transformer (AdDiff-GT), partial observability, meta-learning.

I Introduction

Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm communication network (USNET) have emerged as a promising networking paradigm for disaster response, emergency communications, cooperative sensing, and complex or adversarial operations [1, 2, 3]. However, their dynamic and distributed nature makes them vulnerable to node failures, link disruptions, electromagnetic interference, and malicious attacks. Severe damage can fragment an connected swarm into multiple disconnected clusters, disrupting information exchange and degrading network connectivity. Thus, autonomous topology recovery is essential for resilient USNET operation[4, 5].

Existing resilient UAV network studies have progressed from connectivity restoration to multidimensional resilience involving communication capacity, resource constraints, coverage, quality of service (QoS), and adversarial conditions [6, 7, 5, 8]. Representative topology-recovery strategies include local interaction and bio-inspired swarm behaviors [9], recovery controlled by software-defined networking  [10], Delaunay triangulation for relay placement [11], virtual coordinate-based topology maintenance [12], and robust relay repositioning [13]. Recent studies have further incorporated coverage preservation and QoS guarantees into connectivity restoration [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. However, reliance on centralized optimization, explicit topology information, or repeated planning limits scalability under severe partitioning. Moreover, connectivity-driven repositioning may cause UAV aggregation and degrade spatial distribution, requiring self-healing to jointly consider connectivity, spatial preservation, and online efficiency.

Severe network damage limits global observability from fragmented local observations. Related studies have highlighted partial observability [19] and multi-level damage awareness [20]. However, conventional monitoring depends on continuous collection of node positions and link states [21], incurring substantial communication overhead and becoming unreliable when complete network information is unavailable [22]. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning and distributed control approaches, such as MADDPG-APF [23], zero-shot physics-guided learning [24], and spatio-temporal aggregation [25, 26], mainly address scalable decision-making and distributed execution rather than the preceding global damage-state inference problem. Therefore, reconstructing global failure states from sparse local observations without continuous transmission of location-sensitive information remains insufficiently addressed.

Graph learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for UAV network recovery and resilient swarm control [4, 19, 20, 27, 28, 17]. Graph neural networks (GNNs) and graph attention networks (GATs) have been widely adopted to learn topology-aware representations for graph-based recovery [29, 28], including graph reinforcement learning under partial observability  [19, 27] and multi-branch damage attention for damage-state modeling [20]. Graph learning has also been extended to recovery planning through online GCN-based recovery with meta-learning [4], GAT-DRL-based joint neighbor selection and trajectory planning [28], and energy-constrained graph convolutional networks (GCNs) recovery  [30]. Other recent efforts have explored zero-shot physics-guided learning [24], distributed hybrid MADDPG-APF frameworks [23], spatio-temporal attention aggregation  [25], and heterogeneous GNNs for IoT-assisted systems [26] to improve scalability and support distributed execution.

Despite these advances, graph-based recovery methods remain challenged by severely partitioned, large-scale USNET. Local message propagation has limited capability to capture long-range dependencies among disconnected clusters, while separate treatment of intra-cluster preservation and inter-cluster coordination may cause inefficient reconnection and excessive spatial aggregation. Moreover, models trained on specific scales or damage distributions often require costly online optimization for unseen scenarios. These gaps motivate a unified framework for global damage-state inference, UAV- and cluster-level topology modeling, and efficient cross-scenario adaptation.

To address these challenges, we develop an integrated self-healing framework for partially observable USNET based on an advection-diffusion graph Transformer (AdDiff-GT). A damage-state perception mechanism infers the global post-damage state from sparse local reports without sharing location-sensitive coordinates. A node-supernode hybrid graph captures intra-cluster structures and inter-cluster relationships. AdDiff-GT then combines local message propagation with global attention, where advection-diffusion dynamics [31] provide a physics-inspired inductive bias for topology recovery. A meta-learning framework transfers recovery knowledge across damage patterns and swarm scales, reducing online planning overhead and enabling distributed airborne inference. A weighted composite loss further balances connectivity restoration, maneuvering cost, motion consistency, inter-cluster coordination, and spatial preservation.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: (i) We formulate resilient self-healing for severely partitioned USNET under incomplete damage-state information, jointly considering connectivity, spatial preservation, and online efficiency, and develop sparse-observation-based global damage inference. (ii) We propose AdDiff-GT, a physics-inspired graph Transformer that integrates advection-diffusion dynamics with a node-supernode hybrid graph for local-global topology recovery, trained with a weighted composite loss. (iii) We develop scale-aware meta-learning for efficient online adaptation and distributed airborne inference. (iv) Experiments on 8,000 partitioned scenarios, including 5,000 large-scale cases, demonstrate effective connectivity recovery and spatial dispersion, while meta-initialization reduces online planning latency with a moderate increase in recovery steps.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system model and problem formulation. Section III describes damage assessment and air-ground asymmetric recovery. Section IV presents the proposed AdDiff-GT framework and fast adaptation. Section V provides the experimental evaluation. Section VI concludes this paper.

Definitions of the main symbols and operators used in this paper are provided in Appendix A.

II System Model and Problem Formulation

II-A UAV Swarm and Communication Architecture

Consider a USNET consisting of NN UAVs. The three-dimensional (3D) position of UAV ii at time tt is denoted by 𝐩i,t=[xi,t,yi,t,zi,t]T∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{i,t}=[x_{i,t},y_{i,t},z_{i,t}]^{\mathrm{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, and its motion state is defined as 𝐱i,t=[𝐩i,tT,si,t]T\mathbf{x}_{i,t}=\left[\mathbf{p}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{T}},s_{i,t}\right]^{\mathrm{T}}, where si,t∈{0,vmov}s_{i,t}\in\{0,v_{\mathrm{mov}}\} represents whether UAV ii is stationary or executing recovery maneuvers at a constant speed vmovv_{\mathrm{mov}}.

II-A1 Hierarchical Communication Architecture

The USNET adopts a hierarchical communication architecture comprising short-range information interaction links (SIILs) and long-range data transmission links (LDTLs). SIILs support local information exchange and intra-swarm topology construction, whereas LDTLs provide a low-rate air-ground control channel between the GCS and surviving UAVs for post-damage coordination. This channel carries the exchange of disconnected-neighbor IDs, inferred damage information, model parameters, and recovery commands.

Under adversarial conditions, post-damage air-ground communication is restricted to ID-level state information and model-level parameter updates to limit the exposure of location-sensitive information. In particular, surviving UAVs do not transmit real-time coordinates or recovery trajectories to the GCS. Instead, spatial information is maintained in a GCS-side virtual topology for global damage-state inference and online model adaptation, reducing location-sensitive information exposure while preserving closed-loop self-healing.

II-A2 Communication Links

The inter-UAV and UAV-to-GCS communication channels are modeled as air-to-air (A2A) and air-to-ground (A2G) links, corresponding to SIILs and LDTLs, respectively.

A2A Links: A line-of-sight (LoS) propagation model is adopted for inter-UAV communication [32]. The received power from UAV jj to UAV ii is given by

where PtxP_{\mathrm{tx}} is the transmission power, GiG_{i} and GjG_{j} are the antenna gains, λ\lambda is the carrier wavelength, di​j,t=‖𝐩i,t−𝐩j,t‖2d_{ij,t}=\|\mathbf{p}_{i,t}-\mathbf{p}_{j,t}\|_{2} is the Euclidean distance between UAVs ii and jj, and |hi​j,t|2|h_{ij,t}|^{2} denotes the small-scale fading gain. An A2A link is established when the received power exceeds the sensitivity threshold τ\tau, i.e., Pi​j,tA2A≥τP^{\mathrm{A2A}}_{ij,t}\geq\tau, which is equivalently characterized by

‖𝐩i,t−𝐩j,t‖2≤Rc,\|\mathbf{p}_{i,t}-\mathbf{p}_{j,t}\|_{2}\leq R_{c}, (2)

where RcR_{c} denotes the effective communication radius. Thus, Eq. (2) defines the physical edge criterion for constructing the intra-swarm topology and evaluating connectivity recovery.

A2G Links: A large-scale fading model is adopted for GCS-UAV communication [33]. The received power at the GCS from UAV ii is modeled as

Pi,tA2G=Ptx​β0​di,t−α​χ,P_{i,t}^{\mathrm{A2G}}=P_{\mathrm{tx}}\beta_{0}d_{i,t}^{-\alpha}\chi, (3)

where β0\beta_{0} denotes the channel gain at the reference distance, di,td_{i,t} is the distance between UAV ii and the GCS, α\alpha is the path loss exponent, and χ\chi represents the shadow fading factor. The A2G link is available when Pi,tA2Gσ2≥γ\frac{P_{i,t}^{\mathrm{A2G}}}{\sigma^{2}}\geq\gamma, where σ2\sigma^{2} is the noise power and γ\gamma is the signal-to-noise ratio threshold. A2G links are used solely for GCS-assisted control and do not participate in intra-swarm topology construction or connectivity recovery.

II-B Residual UAV (RUAV) Graph Construction

Let the intact USNET at time tt be represented by 𝒢t=(𝒱t,ℰt,𝐗t)\mathcal{G}_{t}=(\mathcal{V}_{t},\mathcal{E}_{t},\mathbf{X}_{t}). Following an unpredictable extreme disaster (UED), let ℛt⊆𝒱t\mathcal{R}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{t} denote the set of surviving UAVs. We assume that all surviving UAVs can report their status to the GCS through backhaul links. The resulting RUAV graph is defined as 𝒢t′=(ℛt,ℰt′,𝐗t′)\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t}=(\mathcal{R}_{t},\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{t},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{t}), where ℰt′={(i,j)∣i,j∈ℛt,i≠j,∥𝐩i,t−𝐩j,t∥2≤Rc}\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{t}=\{(i,j)\mid i,j\in\mathcal{R}_{t},\ i\neq j,\ \|\mathbf{p}_{i,t}-\mathbf{p}_{j,t}\|_{2}\leq R_{c}\}, and 𝐗t′=[𝐩r1,t,…,𝐩r|ℛt|,t]T\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{t}=[\mathbf{p}_{r_{1},t},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{r_{|\mathcal{R}_{t}|},t}]^{\mathrm{T}} denotes the position matrix of the surviving UAVs. Thus, 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t} characterizes the post-damage communication topology. If 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t} forms a single connected cluster, the surviving UAVs retain global communication capability; otherwise, the RUAV network is partitioned into multiple disconnected clusters, which must be reconnected through cooperative UAV repositioning.

Let 𝐀t=(ai​j,t)\mathbf{A}_{t}=(a_{ij,t}) denote the adjacency matrix of 𝒢t′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t}, where ai​j,t=1a_{ij,t}=1 if (i,j)∈ℰt′(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{t} and ai​j,t=0a_{ij,t}=0 otherwise. The corresponding degree matrix is 𝐃t=diag⁡(∑ja1​j,t,…,∑ja|ℛt|​j,t)\mathbf{D}_{t}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\sum_{j}a_{1j,t},\ldots,\sum_{j}a_{|\mathcal{R}_{t}|j,t}\right), and the graph Laplacian matrix is 𝐋t=𝐃t−𝐀t\mathbf{L}_{t}=\mathbf{D}_{t}-\mathbf{A}_{t}.
